questions.q: What is the most common root cause of hitting the 100-SOQL-query-per-transaction governor limit?
options: Using GROUP BY without HAVING
Using too many WHERE clause conditions in a single query
A SOQL query placed inside a for loop, running once per iteration instead of once total
Selecting too few fields in the SELECT list
questions.explain: Running a query inside a loop multiplies the number of queries issued by the number of loop iterations — the standard fix is to query once, outside the loop.

questions.q: What is the total governor limit for rows retrieved by SOQL queries in a single synchronous transaction?
options: There is no row limit, only a query count limit
2,000 rows
100 rows
50,000 rows
questions.explain: 50,000 total rows retrieved by SOQL queries is the governor limit per transaction, for both synchronous and asynchronous contexts.

questions.q: How does a parent-to-child relationship subquery affect a query's cost against governor limits?
options: Each parent-child relationship counts as an extra query, with relationship subqueries getting a combined budget of 3x the top-level query limit
Relationship subqueries are entirely free and never count against any limit
Relationship subqueries count as SOSL searches instead of SOQL queries
Only the first relationship subquery in a query counts against the limit
questions.explain: Salesforce documents that each parent-child relationship in a query counts as an extra query, with a combined cap of three times the top-level query limit.

questions.q: Why does a leading wildcard, e.g. LIKE '%term%', hurt query performance on a large object?
options: It is a syntax error and the query won't run at all
It prevents index use, since there's no fixed starting point for an index to narrow from
It forces the query to run as a SOSL search instead
It only affects queries using GROUP BY
questions.explain: A leading % wildcard means the match could start anywhere in the string, which an index can't use to narrow the search the way a prefix match could.

questions.q: Why doesn't a query performing fine against 50 test records guarantee it will perform fine in production?
options: Test records are always indexed differently than production records
Governor limits only apply in sandboxes, not in production
An unselective filter that doesn't matter at small scale can force a full object scan at large scale
SOQL behaves completely differently depending on the org's edition
questions.explain: A filter's selectivity — how large a fraction of the table it matches — only becomes a real performance factor once the table is large enough for index usage to matter.
